markscheme: (a) $r_A=0.947$ [A1] $r_B=0.923$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) enter all eight points together [M1] $r=-0.765$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) group $A$ has larger $y$-values but smaller $x$-values than group $B$ [R1] so combining them creates a downward trend even though each group rises [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Calculate each correlation separately and then for the pooled data. A hidden grouping variable can reverse the apparent direction of a relationship.

subtopic: Comparing predictors using correlation coefficients
statement: A teacher calculates the correlation between students' exam scores and three other variables: hours of sleep, $r=0.46$; hours of study, $r=0.81$; number of absences, $r=-0.88$. (a) State which variable has the strongest linear relationship with exam score. [1] (b) State what the sign of the relationship with absences tells you. [1] (c) The teacher concludes that making students study more will increase their scores. Comment on this conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) number of absences, since $|-0.88|$ is the largest [A1] [1 mark] (b) more absences are associated with lower exam scores [A1] [1 mark] (c) the data show a strong positive association [A1] but correlation alone does not show that studying causes the higher scores [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Compare the magnitudes $|r|$ for strength, and use the sign for direction.

subtopic: Regression for equally spaced values of x
statement: A plant's height $y$ cm is recorded at the end of each of $6$ weeks, $x=1,2,\ldots,6$: $12,\ 15,\ 19,\ 20,\ 24,\ 27$. (a) Show that $\sum(x-\bar x)^2=17.5$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (c) Estimate the height after $8$ weeks, and comment on the reliability of the estimate. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=3.5$ [A1] $2(2.5^2+1.5^2+0.5^2)=17.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) gradient $=\dfrac{\sum(x-\bar x)y}{17.5}=\dfrac{51.5}{17.5}$ [M1] $=2.94$ [A1] $y=2.94x+9.20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2.94\times8+9.20=32.7$ cm [A1] week $8$ is beyond the range of the data, so it may be unreliable [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For equally spaced $x$-values, the sum of squares $\sum(x-\bar x)^2$ is a quick calculation, and $\sum(x-\bar x)\bar y=0$.

subtopic: A line fitted by eye compared with the regression line
statement: A student has the data $(2,15),\ (4,22),\ (6,31),\ (8,38),\ (10,47)$ and draws a line of best fit by eye through the points $(2,15)$ and $(10,47)$. (a) Find the equation of the student's line. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) Compare the two predictions at $x=7$, and state which line passes through the mean point. [3]
markscheme: (a) gradient $\dfrac{47-15}{10-2}=4$ [M1][A1] $y=4x+7$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=4x+6.6$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (c) student: $4\times7+7=35$ [A1] regression: $4\times7+6.6=34.6$ [A1] the regression line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)=(6,30.6)$, while the student's line gives $31$ at $x=6$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The regression line always passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$, which a line drawn by eye need not do.

subtopic: Using a regression line to find when a value is exceeded
statement: The number of subscribers $y$ (in thousands) to a streaming service is modeled by $y=12.4x+150$, where $x$ is the number of months since the start of 2023. The model was fitted using data for $x=1,2,\ldots,12$. (a) Interpret the values $12.4$ and $150$ in this context. [2] (b) Find the first month in which the model predicts more than $500$ thousand subscribers. [3] (c) Explain why this prediction may not be reliable. [1]
markscheme: (a) subscribers grow by $12\,400$ per month [A1] $150\,000$ subscribers at the start (when $x=0$) [A1] [2 marks] (b) $12.4x+150>500$ [M1] $x>28.2$ [A1] month $29$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) month $29$ is well outside the data range $1$ to $12$ (extrapolation) [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Solve the inequality, then round up to the next whole month, since $x$ counts completed months.

subtopic: Zero correlation despite an exact relationship
statement: The seven points $(-3,9),\ (-2,4),\ (-1,1),\ (0,0),\ (1,1),\ (2,4),\ (3,9)$ all satisfy $y=x^2$. (a) Use your calculator to find the Pearson correlation coefficient and the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Explain why the value of $r$ does not mean that there is no relationship between $x$ and $y$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=0$ [A1] regression line $y=4$ (gradient $0$, mean of $y$) [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $r$ measures only the strength of a linear relationship [R1] the points follow an exact quadratic relationship, symmetric about $x=0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Always inspect a scatter diagram: a correlation coefficient of 0 can hide a strong non-linear pattern.

subtopic: Effect of linear changes of units on the correlation coefficient
statement: For variables $x$ and $y$ with covariance $s_{xy}$ and standard deviations $s_x$ and $s_y$, new variables are defined by $u=ax+b$ and $v=cy+d$, where $a,c\ne0$. (a) Show that the covariance of $u$ and $v$ is $ac\,s_{xy}$. [2] (b) Write down the standard deviations of $u$ and $v$, and hence show that $r_{uv}=\dfrac{ac}{|ac|}r_{xy}$. [3] (c) Heights are converted from centimeters to inches ($u=0.394x$) and masses from kilograms to pounds ($v=2.20y$). State the effect on the correlation coefficient. [1] (d) State the effect on $r$ of using $v=-y$ instead. [1]
markscheme: (a) $u-\bar u=a(x-\bar x)$ and $v-\bar v=c(y-\bar y)$ [M1] mean of the product $=ac\,s_{xy}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $s_u=|a|s_x$ and $s_v=|c|s_y$ [A1] $r_{uv}=\dfrac{ac\,s_{xy}}{|a||c|s_xs_y}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{ac}{|ac|}r_{xy}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) both multipliers are positive, so $r$ is unchanged [R1] [1 mark] (d) $\dfrac{ac}{|ac|}=-1$, so $r$ changes sign but keeps its magnitude [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Subtracting the means removes $b$ and $d$. The positive scale factors cancel between numerator and denominator, leaving only a possible sign change.

subtopic: Adding a point that lies on the regression line
statement: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the five points $(1,3),\ (2,5),\ (3,4),\ (4,8),\ (5,9)$ is $y=1.5x+1.3$, and $\bar x=3$, $\bar y=5.8$. A sixth point $P(6,10.3)$ is added. (a) Show that $P$ lies on the original regression line. [1] (b) Find the new means $\bar x$ and $\bar y$, and show that the new mean point lies on the original line. [3] (c) Using $\sum(x-\bar x)^2=17.5$ for all six points and $\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=26.25$, find the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for the six points. [3] (d) Explain, without further calculation, why the line is unchanged when a point lying on the line is added. [3] (e) The correlation coefficient of the original five points is $0.916$. Find the correlation coefficient for the six points, given that $\sum(y-\bar y)^2=43.675$, and comment. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1.5\times6+1.3=10.3$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) $\bar x=\dfrac{15+6}6=3.5$ [A1] $\bar y=\dfrac{29+10.3}6=6.55$ [A1] $1.5\times3.5+1.3=6.55$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) gradient $=\dfrac{26.25}{17.5}=1.5$ [M1][A1] passes through $(3.5,6.55)$ so $y=1.5x+1.3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the regression line minimizes the sum of squared vertical distances [R1] the new point contributes a squared distance of $0$ on the old line [R1] the old line already minimized the other terms, so it still gives the minimum [R1] [3 marks] (e) $r=\dfrac{26.25}{\sqrt{17.5\times43.675}}$ [M1][A1] $=0.949$ [A1] $r$ has increased, since the new point fits the pattern perfectly and extends the range of the data [R1] [4 marks]
tips: The regression line is the line minimizing the total squared vertical distance. A point that already lies on the line adds nothing to that total.

subtopic: Comparing two linear models
statement: The values (in dollars) of two types of car $t$ years after purchase are modeled by $A=24000-2100t$ and $B=19500-1500t$. (a) Interpret the gradient of each model. [2] (b) Find when the two models give the same value, and state which car is worth more before then. [3] (c) Find the time at which each model predicts a value of zero, and state which model is meaningful for longer. [3]
markscheme: (a) car $A$ loses $\$2100$ per year [A1] car $B$ loses $\$1500$ per year [A1] [2 marks] (b) $24000-2100t=19500-1500t$ [M1] $t=7.5$ years [A1] car $A$ is worth more for $t<7.5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A=0$ at $t=\dfrac{24000}{2100}=11.4$ years [A1] $B=0$ at $t=\dfrac{19500}{1500}=13$ years [A1] $B$ is meaningful for longer [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Set the two expressions equal to find the crossover, and set each equal to zero to find where it stops being sensible.

subtopic: The mean of the predicted values equals the mean of y
statement: Four observations are $(2,5),\ (4,9),\ (6,10),\ (8,16)$. The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=1.7x+1.5$. (a) Calculate the four predicted values of $y$ given by the line. [2] (b) Show that the mean of the predicted values is equal to the mean of the observed $y$-values. [2] (c) Explain why this is true for every regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $4.9,\ 8.3,\ 11.7,\ 15.1$ [M1][A1] [2 marks] (b) mean of predicted values $=\dfrac{40}4=10$ [A1] $\bar y=\dfrac{40}4=10$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the mean of $a+bx_i$ is $a+b\bar x$ [M1] the line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ so this equals $\bar y$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The regression line passes through the mean point, so substituting $\bar x$ gives $\bar y$.

subtopic: When a large correlation coefficient is misleading
statement: The values of $x$ and $y$ are $(1,100),\ (2,60),\ (3,35),\ (4,20),\ (5,12),\ (6,9)$. The correlation coefficient is $r=-0.93$, and the regression line is $y=100.7-17.5x$. (a) State what the value of $r$ suggests about the relationship. [1] (b) Use the regression line to predict $y$ when $x=8$, and explain why this prediction shows that the linear model is inappropriate. [3] (c) Explain why a high value of $|r|$ does not by itself show that a linear model is suitable. [1]
markscheme: (a) a strong negative linear association [A1] [1 mark] (b) $100.7-17.5\times8=-39.3$ [A1] a negative value is not consistent with the values of $y$, which are positive and levelling off [R1] the data decrease at a decreasing rate, which is curved, not linear [R1] [3 marks] (c) $r$ measures only linear association; curved data can still give a large $|r|$, so a scatter diagram should be examined [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Check the shape of the data, not only the value of $r$. Predictions that are impossible in context show the model has failed.

subtopic: Energy use and temperature: regression, prediction and limits
statement: A building's daily energy use $y$ (in kWh) and the average outdoor temperature $x$ ($^\circ$C) are recorded on $7$ days: $(2,88),\ (5,79),\ (8,70),\ (11,61),\ (14,55),\ (17,44),\ (20,37)$. (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient and the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [3] (b) Predict the energy use on a day when the average temperature is $12^\circ$C. [2] (c) The line predicts $-6.0$ kWh at $35^\circ$C. Explain why this prediction is not valid. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=-0.999$ [A1] $y=-2.83x+93.2$ [M1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $-2.83\times12+93.2$ [M1] $=59.2$ kWh [A1] [2 marks] (c) extrapolation beyond the data range ($2$ to $20$), and energy use cannot be negative [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Use the two-variable statistics function of your calculator. Interpolation within the range of the data is more reliable than extrapolation.

subtopic: Solving z squared equals the conjugate of z
statement: Consider the equation $z^2=z^*$, where $z\in\mathbb C$ and $z^*$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. (a) By taking moduli, show that either $z=0$ or $|z|=1$. [3] (b) When $|z|=1$, show that $z^3=1$, and hence find all the solutions of $z^2=z^*$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $|z|^2=|z^*|=|z|$ [M1] so $|z|(|z|-1)=0$ [A1] hence $z=0$ or $|z|=1$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^*=\dfrac1z$ since $zz^*=|z|^2=1$ [M1] so $z^2=\dfrac1z$ and $z^3=1$ [A1] $z=1$ or $z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{2\pi}3\right)=-\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] with $z=0$ the solutions are $0,\ 1,\ -\dfrac12\pm\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: For a number of modulus 1, the conjugate equals the reciprocal, because $zz^*=|z|^2$.

subtopic: Exact value of cos 15 degrees from a complex quotient
statement: Let $w=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm i}{1+\mathrm i}$. (a) Write $w$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$, with $a$ and $b$ in exact form. [3] (b) Write $1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm i$ and $1+\mathrm i$ in modulus-argument form, and hence show that $w=\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi{12}+\mathrm i\sin\dfrac\pi{12}\right)$. [3] (c) Hence find the exact value of $\cos\dfrac\pi{12}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{(1+\sqrt3\mathrm i)(1-\mathrm i)}{2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3+(\sqrt3-1)\mathrm i}2$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $1+\sqrt3\mathrm i=2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi3$ and $1+\mathrm i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$ [A1][A1] divide moduli, subtract arguments, $\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac\pi{12}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (c) equate real parts: $\sqrt2\cos\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{1+\sqrt3}2$ [M1] $\cos\dfrac\pi{12}=\dfrac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rationalize the denominator by multiplying by the conjugate, and separately divide in polar form. Equate the two expressions for $w$.

subtopic: Region defined by a modulus and an argument
statement: The region $R$ in the complex plane is the set of points $z$ with $|z|\le2$ and $\dfrac\pi6\le\arg z\le\dfrac\pi2$. (a) Find the area of $R$. [2] (b) Find the perimeter of $R$. [2] (c) Determine whether the point $1.5+0.5\mathrm i$ lies in $R$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $R$ is a sector of radius $2$ and angle $\dfrac\pi2-\dfrac\pi6=\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] area $=\dfrac12\times4\times\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) arc length $2\times\dfrac\pi3$ [M1] perimeter $=2+2+\dfrac{2\pi}3=4+\dfrac{2\pi}3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\arg=\arctan\dfrac13=0.322$ [M1] this is less than $\dfrac\pi6=0.524$, so it is not in $R$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The modulus condition gives a disc of radius 2 and the argument condition cuts a wedge from it. Together they form a sector.

subtopic: Quartic equation solved as a quadratic in z squared
statement: Consider the equation $z^4-2z^2+4=0$, where $z\in\mathbb C$. (a) Solve the equation for $z^2$, and write each value in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [3] (b) Hence find the four solutions for $z$ in the form $a+b\mathrm i$, with $a$ and $b$ exact. [4]
markscheme: (a) $z^2=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}2$ [M1] $=1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i$ [A1] $=2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi6\right)$ [M1][A1] and the negatives of these [M1] $z=\pm\left(\dfrac{\sqrt6}2\pm\dfrac{\sqrt2}2\mathrm i\right)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Treat $z^2$ as the unknown. The square roots of a complex number come in pairs differing by a sign.

subtopic: Proof that the modulus of a product is the product of moduli
statement: Let $z_1=a+b\mathrm i$ and $z_2=c+d\mathrm i$, where $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $|z_1z_2|^2=(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)$, and hence that $|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|$. [4] (b) Use the result to show that $\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\dfrac1{|z|}$ for $z\ne0$. [2] (c) Hence find $\left|\dfrac{(3+4\mathrm i)^5}{(1-\sqrt3\mathrm i)^3}\right|$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z_1z_2=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathrm i$ [M1] $|z_1z_2|^2=(ac-bd)^2+(ad+bc)^2$ [A1] $=a^2c^2+b^2d^2+a^2d^2+b^2c^2=(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)$ [A1] take square roots (both sides non-negative) [R1] [4 marks] (b) $|z|\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\left|z\times\dfrac1z\right|=|1|=1$ [M1] so $\left|\dfrac1z\right|=\dfrac1{|z|}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{5^5}{2^3}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{3125}8$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expand the product in Cartesian form, then compare with the product of the two sums of squares.

subtopic: Solving z + 1/z = 1 and a high power
statement: The complex number $z$ satisfies $z+\dfrac1z=1$. (a) Show that $z^2-z+1=0$, and find the two possible values of $z$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [3] (b) Show that $z^3=-1$ for both values. [2] (c) Hence find $z^{2025}$. [2]
markscheme: (a) multiply by $z$: $z^2+1=z$ [M1] $z=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt3\mathrm i}2$ [A1] $z=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi3\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $z^3+1=(z+1)(z^2-z+1)=0$ [M1] since $z\ne-1$ ($z=-1$ gives $-2\ne1$), $z^3=-1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $2025=3\times675$ [M1] $z^{2025}=(-1)^{675}=-1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiply through by $z$ to get a quadratic. The factorization of $z^3+1$ links the quadratic to the cube.

subtopic: Sixth roots of -64 and real quadratic factors
statement: Consider the equation $z^6=-64$. (a) Find the six solutions in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ with $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. [3] (b) Write the solutions in the form $a+b\mathrm i$. [2] (c) Hence factorize $z^6+64$ into three real quadratic factors. [3] (d) Find the product of the six roots, and verify it with the constant term of the polynomial. [2]
markscheme: (a) $|z|=2$ [A1] $\arg z=\dfrac{\pi+2k\pi}6$ [M1] $2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi6\right),\ 2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac\pi2\right),\ 2\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\dfrac{5\pi}6\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\pm\sqrt3\pm\mathrm i$ [A1] $\pm2\mathrm i$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) each conjugate pair gives a real quadratic [M1] $z^2+4$ [A1] $(z^2-2\sqrt3z+4)(z^2+2\sqrt3z+4)$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) modulus $2^6=64$ [A1] sum of arguments $=0$, and the product of the roots of $z^6+64$ equals $+64$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: For real coefficients the non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs. A pair $p\pm q\mathrm i$ gives the quadratic factor $z^2-2pz+p^2+q^2$.

subtopic: Multiplication by a complex number as a rotation and enlargement
statement: A triangle has vertices at the points $1,\ 3$ and $3+2\mathrm i$ in the complex plane. Each vertex $z$ is mapped to $w=(1+\mathrm i)z$. (a) Describe the transformation as a rotation followed by an enlargement, giving the angle and the scale factor. [2] (b) Find the images of the three vertices. [3] (c) Find the area of the original triangle, and use the scale factor to find the area of the image. [3]
markscheme: (a) $1+\mathrm i=\sqrt2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac\pi4$ [M1] rotation of $\dfrac\pi4$ anticlockwise about the origin, enlargement with scale factor $\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1+\mathrm i$ [A1] $3+3\mathrm i$ [A1] $(3+2\mathrm i)(1+\mathrm i)=1+5\mathrm i$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) base $2$, height $2$, area $=2$ [A1] area scale factor $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ [M1] image area $=4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ rotates by $\theta$ and enlarges lengths by $r$, so areas are multiplied by $r^2$.

subtopic: Finding a complex number with a given product and modulus
statement: Let $z_1=3+4\mathrm i$. (a) Find the two complex numbers $z_2$ for which $z_1z_2$ is a real number and $|z_2|=10$. [4] (b) Find the two complex numbers $z_2$ for which $z_1z_2$ is purely imaginary and $|z_2|=10$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $z_1z_2$ real means $z_2$ is a real multiple of $z_1^*=3-4\mathrm i$ [M1] $z_2=k(3-4\mathrm i)$ [A1] $5|k|=10$ so $k=\pm2$ [M1] $z_2=\pm(6-8\mathrm i)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $z_2$ is a real multiple of $\mathrm iz_1^*=4+3\mathrm i$ [M1] $|z_2|=10$ gives $z_2=\pm2(4+3\mathrm i)$ [M1] $=\pm(8+6\mathrm i)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A product $z_1z_2$ is real when the arguments of $z_1$ and $z_2$ cancel. Multiplying by $z_1^*$ gives a real number.

subtopic: Modulus and argument of 1 + e^(i theta)
statement: Let $\theta$ be a real number with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. (a) Show that $1+e^{\mathrm i\theta}=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$. [3] (b) Hence write down the modulus and argument of $1+e^{\mathrm i\theta}$. [2] (c) Find the modulus and argument of $1+\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{5\pi}6$, giving the modulus exactly. [3]
markscheme: (a) factor out $e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$: $e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}\left(e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}+e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}\right)$ [M1][A1] $=2\cos\dfrac\theta2\,e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) modulus $2\cos\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] argument $\dfrac\theta2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}6$, argument $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] modulus $2\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Pull out half of the angle, so that the exponentials combine into a cosine. The factor is positive only for $|\theta|<\pi$, which is why the modulus is $2\cos(\theta/2)$.

subtopic: Real and imaginary quotients with an unknown parameter
statement: Let $w=\dfrac{a+2\mathrm i}{1-\mathrm i}$, where $a$ is a real number. (a) Write $w$ in the form $x+y\mathrm i$, with $x,y$ in terms of $a$. [2] (b) Find the value of $a$ for which $w$ is real, and the value for which $w$ is purely imaginary. [2] (c) For $a=0$, find the modulus and argument of $w$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{(a+2\mathrm i)(1+\mathrm i)}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{a-2}2+\dfrac{a+2}2\mathrm i$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) real: $a+2=0$ so $a=-2$ [A1] purely imaginary: $a-2=0$ so $a=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $w=-1+\mathrm i$ [A1] modulus $\sqrt2$ [A1] argument $\dfrac{3\pi}4$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator to separate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Intersection of a circle and a ray in the complex plane
statement: Consider the locus $|z-2-2\mathrm i|=2$ and the half-line $\arg z=\dfrac\pi4$. (a) Describe each of the two loci geometrically. [2] (b) Write $z=t(1+\mathrm i)$ with $t>0$, and find the values of $z$ that lie on both loci, in exact form. [4]
markscheme: (a) circle with centre $(2,2)$ and radius $2$ [A1] half-line from the origin at $45^\circ$ to the positive real axis, along $y=x$ with $x>0$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $|(t-2)(1+\mathrm i)|=2$ [M1] $\sqrt2|t-2|=2$ [A1] $t=2\pm\sqrt2$, both positive [A1] $z=(2\pm\sqrt2)(1+\mathrm i)$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Points on the ray $\arg z=\pi/4$ have the form $t(1+\mathrm i)$ with $t>0$. Substitute into the equation of the circle.

subtopic: The triple angle tangent formula from de Moivre
statement: Let $t=\tan\theta$. (a) Use de Moivre's theorem to show that $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}$. [4] (b) Hence show that $\tan\theta$ satisfies $t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$ when $\tan3\theta=1$. [2] (c) Solve $\tan3\theta=1$ for $0<\theta<\pi$, and hence find the exact roots of $t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3$ expanded: real part $\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta$ [M1] imaginary part $3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\sin^3\theta$ [A1] $\tan3\theta=\dfrac{\text{Im}}{\text{Re}}$, divide by $\cos^3\theta$ [M1] result [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $3t-t^3=1-3t^2$ [M1] rearrange: $t^3-3t^2-3t+1=0$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $3\theta=\dfrac\pi4,\ \dfrac{5\pi}4,\ \dfrac{9\pi}4$ [M1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{3\pi}4$ [A1] roots are $\tan\dfrac\pi{12}$, $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$, $\tan\dfrac{3\pi}4$ [M1] $2-\sqrt3,\ 2+\sqrt3,\ -1$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Use the real and imaginary parts of $(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3$. The three values of $\theta$ in $(0,\pi)$ give the three roots of the cubic.

subtopic: Vertices of a square using rotation by 90 degrees
statement: In the complex plane, $A$ is the point $1+\mathrm i$ and $B$ is the point $4+2\mathrm i$. The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are the vertices of a square, taken in anticlockwise order. (a) Find the complex number representing $\overrightarrow{AB}$, and explain how $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is obtained from it. [2] (b) Find $C$ and $D$, and the area of the square. [4] (c) The square could instead lie on the other side of $AB$. Find the two corresponding vertices in this case. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=3+\mathrm i$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathrm i\times\overrightarrow{AB}$, a rotation by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise [R1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{BC}=\mathrm i(3+\mathrm i)=-1+3\mathrm i$ [A1] $C=3+5\mathrm i$ [A1] $D=A+\overrightarrow{BC}=4\mathrm i$ [A1] area $=|AB|^2=10$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) multiply $\overrightarrow{AB}$ by $-\mathrm i$: $-\mathrm i(3+\mathrm i)=1-3\mathrm i$ [M1] $C=5-\mathrm i$ and $D=2-2\mathrm i$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Multiplying by $\mathrm i$ rotates a vector by $90^\circ$ anticlockwise, and multiplying by $-\mathrm i$ rotates it clockwise.

subtopic: When is a power of a complex number real
statement: Let $z=1+\sqrt3\,\mathrm i$. (a) Write $z$ in the form $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$. [2] (b) Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which $z^n$ is a positive real number, and the smallest for which $z^n$ is a negative real number. [3] (c) Find the smallest $n$ for which $|z^n|>1000$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $r=2$ [A1] $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $z^n=2^n\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{n\pi}3$ [M1] positive real needs $\dfrac{n\pi}3=2\pi k$, so $n=6$ [A1] negative real needs $\dfrac{n\pi}3=\pi$, so $n=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2^n>1000$ [M1] $n=10$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The argument of $z^n$ is $n\theta$. A number is real when its argument is a multiple of $\pi$.

subtopic: The map w = (z - 1)/(z + 1) and the unit circle
statement: For $z\in\mathbb C$ with $z\ne-1$, define $w=\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}$. (a) Let $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. Show that $w=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\theta2$. [4] (b) Deduce that $w$ traces the whole imaginary axis as $z$ goes around the unit circle (excluding $z=-1$). [2] (c) Let $z=x+y\mathrm i$. Show that $\operatorname{Re}(w)=\dfrac{x^2+y^2-1}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$. [3] (d) Hence describe the image of the region $|z|<1$ under the map, with a reason. [2] (e) Verify the result of part (a) for $z=\mathrm i$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $w=\dfrac{e^{\mathrm i\theta}-1}{e^{\mathrm i\theta}+1}$ [M1] multiply top and bottom by $e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}-e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}}{e^{\mathrm i\theta/2}+e^{-\mathrm i\theta/2}}=\dfrac{2\mathrm i\sin(\theta/2)}{2\cos(\theta/2)}$ [A1] $=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\theta2$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\tan\dfrac\theta2$ takes every real value for $-\pi<\theta<\pi$ [R1] so $w=\mathrm iy$ takes every pure imaginary value [R1] [2 marks] (c) $w=\dfrac{(z-1)(z^*+1)}{|z+1|^2}$ [M1] numerator $=|z|^2+z-z^*-1$ [A1] $z-z^*$ is imaginary, so real part is $\dfrac{x^2+y^2-1}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) the denominator is positive and the numerator is negative when $|z|<1$, so $\operatorname{Re}(w)<0$ [R1] the open unit disc maps into the left half-plane [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{\mathrm i-1}{\mathrm i+1}=\mathrm i=\mathrm i\tan\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Write $z=e^{\mathrm i\theta}$ and use half-angles so that numerator and denominator become $\sin$ and $\cos$ of $\theta/2$.

subtopic: Sum of squared distances between vertices of a regular polygon
statement: The vertices of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in the unit circle are $1,\omega,\omega^2,\ldots,\omega^{n-1}$, where $\omega=\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{2\pi}n$ and $n\ge3$. (a) Show that $|1-\operatorname{cis}\theta|^2=2-2\cos\theta$. [2] (b) Explain why $1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{n-1}=0$, and deduce that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n=-1$. [3] (c) Hence show that the sum of the squares of the distances from the vertex $1$ to the other $n-1$ vertices is $2n$. [3] (d) Verify the result for $n=6$ by finding the distances from the vertex $1$ to the other five vertices. [2] (e) By symmetry, the same result holds for every vertex. Find the sum of the squares of the lengths of all $\dbinom n2$ chords joining pairs of vertices. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta$ [M1] $=2-2\cos\theta$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) geometric series with ratio $\omega\ne1$ and $\omega^n=1$, so the sum is $\dfrac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega}=0$ [M1][R1] real parts give $1+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) distance squared to $\omega^k$ is $2-2\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n$ [A1] sum $=2(n-1)-2\sum\cos\dfrac{2\pi k}n$ [M1] $=2(n-1)+2=2n$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) distances $1,\ \sqrt3,\ 2,\ \sqrt3,\ 1$ [A1] squares sum to $1+3+4+3+1=12=2\times6$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) summing over all $n$ vertices counts each chord twice: $\dfrac{n\times2n}2$ [M1] $=n^2$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A regular polygon's vertices are the $n$th roots of unity, whose sum is zero. Use the cosine form of the distance formula.

subtopic: Logarithmic differentiation of x raised to sin x
statement: Let $y=x^{\sin x}$ for $x>0$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}x\right)$. [4] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=\dfrac\pi2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\ln y=\sin x\ln x$ [M1] $\dfrac1y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos x\ln x+\dfrac{\sin x}x$ [M1][A1] multiply by $y=x^{\sin x}$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=\dfrac\pi2$ at $x=\dfrac\pi2$ [A1] gradient $=\dfrac\pi2\left(0+\dfrac{1}{\pi/2}\right)=1$ [A1] $y-\dfrac\pi2=x-\dfrac\pi2$, so $y=x$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Take natural logarithms of both sides, then differentiate implicitly using the product rule on the right-hand side.

subtopic: Tangent to y = ln x passing through the origin
statement: Consider the curve $y=\ln x$. (a) Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=a$. [2] (b) Find the value of $a$ for which the tangent passes through the origin, and write down the equation of that tangent. [3] (c) Hence state the number of solutions of $\ln x=kx$ when $k=\dfrac1e$. [1]
markscheme: (a) gradient $\dfrac1a$ [A1] $y-\ln a=\dfrac1a(x-a)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $0-\ln a=\dfrac1a(0-a)=-1$ [M1] $\ln a=1$ so $a=e$ [A1] $y=\dfrac xe$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) exactly one solution, $x=e$, since the line is tangent to the curve [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A line through the origin has the form $y=kx$. Substitute the origin into the tangent equation to find the point of tangency.

subtopic: Largest cone inscribed in a sphere
statement: A cone is inscribed in a sphere of radius $6$ cm, with its apex at the top of the sphere and its base a circle on the sphere. The height of the cone is $h$ cm, where $0<h<12$. (a) Show that the radius $r$ of the base satisfies $r^2=h(12-h)$. [2] (b) Show that the volume of the cone is $V=\dfrac\pi3\left(12h^2-h^3\right)$. [1] (c) Find the value of $h$ that maximizes $V$, justify that it is a maximum, and find the maximum volume. [5]
markscheme: (a) a right-angled triangle formed by the sphere's diameter, the apex and a point on the base circle [M1] altitude on the hypotenuse gives $r^2=h(12-h)$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac13\pi r^2h=\dfrac\pi3(12h^2-h^3)$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (c) $\dfrac{dV}{dh}=\dfrac\pi3(24h-3h^2)$ [A1] $=0$ at $h=8$ [M1][A1] $\dfrac{d^2V}{dh^2}=\dfrac\pi3(24-6h)<0$ at $h=8$, so a maximum [R1] $V=\dfrac{256\pi}3=268\text{ cm}^3$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Use the right angle in a semicircle to relate $r$ and $h$. Substitute into the volume formula before differentiating.

subtopic: Window of maximum area for a fixed perimeter
statement: A window is a rectangle of width $2r$ and height $h$ metres, with a semicircle of radius $r$ metres on top of the rectangle's upper side. The perimeter of the whole window (the base, two vertical sides and the semicircular arc) is $12$ m. (a) Show that $h=6-\left(1+\dfrac\pi2\right)r$, and that the area of the window is $A=12r-\left(2+\dfrac\pi2\right)r^2$. [4] (b) Find the value of $r$ that maximizes $A$, and show that $h=r$ for this value. [4] (c) Find the maximum area to three significant figures, with a reason why it is a maximum. [2]
markscheme: (a) perimeter $2r+2h+\pi r=12$ [M1] $h=6-\left(1+\dfrac\pi2\right)r$ [AG] [A1] $A=2rh+\dfrac12\pi r^2$ [M1] $=12r-(2+\pi)r^2+\dfrac\pi2r^2=12r-\left(2+\dfrac\pi2\right)r^2$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=12-(4+\pi)r$ [A1] $=0$ at $r=\dfrac{12}{4+\pi}=1.68$ [A1] $h=6-\dfrac{(2+\pi)r}2$ [M1] $=\dfrac{12-(2+\pi)r}{2}=\dfrac{(4+\pi)r-(2+\pi)r}2=r$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $A=12r-\dfrac{4+\pi}2r^2=6r=10.1\text{ m}^2$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-(4+\pi)<0$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Write the perimeter condition to eliminate $h$, then maximize a quadratic in $r$ by differentiating.

subtopic: Wire cut to form a square and a circle with minimum total area
statement: A wire of length $100$ cm is cut into two pieces. One piece is bent into a square of side $a$ cm, and the other into a circle of radius $r$ cm. (a) Express $r$ in terms of $a$, and show that the total area is $A=a^2+\dfrac{(100-4a)^2}{4\pi}$. [3] (b) Find the value of $a$ that minimizes the total area, and the minimum area. [5] (c) Find the total area when the whole wire is used for the square, and when it is used for the circle, and comment. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4a+2\pi r=100$ [M1] $r=\dfrac{100-4a}{2\pi}$ [A1] $A=a^2+\pi r^2=a^2+\dfrac{(100-4a)^2}{4\pi}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac{dA}{da}=2a-\dfrac{2(100-4a)}{\pi}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ gives $a\pi=100-4a$, so $a=\dfrac{100}{\pi+4}=14.0$ [A1] $A=350\text{ cm}^2$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2A}{da^2}=2+\dfrac8\pi>0$, so a minimum [R1] [5 marks] (c) all square: $25^2=625$ [A1] all circle: $\pi\left(\dfrac{50}\pi\right)^2=796$ [A1] the minimum $350$ lies below both, so the greatest area occurs at an extreme and the stationary point is a minimum [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Eliminate $r$ using the length of wire, then differentiate the area as a function of $a$ only.

subtopic: Rate of change of the distance between two ships
statement: Ship $A$ is $60$ km west of a lighthouse and sails east at $20$ km/h. At the same time, ship $B$ is $80$ km south of the lighthouse and sails north at $15$ km/h. Let $s$ be the distance between the ships after $t$ hours. (a) Show that $s^2=(60-20t)^2+(80-15t)^2$. [2] (b) Find the rate of change of $s$ when $t=1$. [4] (c) State what the sign of your answer means. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A$ is $60-20t$ km from the lighthouse along the east-west line [A1] $B$ is $80-15t$ km along the north-south line, and the two lines are perpendicular so Pythagoras applies [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2s\dfrac{ds}{dt}=-40(60-20t)-30(80-15t)$ [M1][A1] at $t=1$: $s=\sqrt{40^2+65^2}=76.3$ [A1] $\dfrac{ds}{dt}=\dfrac{-1600-1950}{2\times76.3}=-23.3$ km/h [A1] [4 marks] (c) the ships are getting closer [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Differentiate the equation for $s^2$ implicitly with respect to $t$. A negative rate means the distance is decreasing.

subtopic: Second derivative by implicit differentiation
statement: A curve has equation $2x^2+y^2=18$. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2x}y$. [2] (b) Show that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{36}{y^3}$. [4] (c) Find the gradient and the value of $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ at the point $(1,4)$, and state what the second derivative says about the curve there. [3]
markscheme: (a) $4x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ [M1] $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2x}y$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{2y-2x\frac{dy}{dx}}{y^2}$ [M1][A1] substitute $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$: $-\dfrac{2y+4x^2/y}{y^2}=-\dfrac{2y^2+4x^2}{y^3}$ [A1] $2y^2+4x^2=2(2x^2+y^2)=36$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) gradient $=-\dfrac24=-\dfrac12$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{36}{64}=-\dfrac9{16}$ [A1] the curve is concave down (it is the upper part of an ellipse) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the quotient rule when differentiating $-2x/y$ a second time, and remember that $dy/dx$ appears again.

subtopic: Stationary points and inflections of x squared times e to the minus x
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2e^{-x}$ for $x\ge0$. (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f$, and determine their nature. [5] (b) Show that $f''(x)=(x^2-4x+2)e^{-x}$ and find the $x$-coordinates of the points of inflection. [4] (c) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the graph. [1]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=2$ [A1] $f(0)=0$ minimum and $f(2)=4e^{-2}$ maximum [M1] by the sign of $f'$: negative then positive at $0$, positive then negative at $2$ [A1] [5 marks] (b) $f''=(2-2x)e^{-x}-(2x-x^2)e^{-x}$ [M1][A1] $=(x^2-4x+2)e^{-x}$ [AG] $x^2-4x+2=0$ [M1] $x=2\pm\sqrt2$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $y=0$ as $x\to\infty$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Factor out $e^{-x}$ after each differentiation. Inflection points need a sign change in $f''$.

subtopic: Continuity and differentiability of a piecewise function
statement: A function is defined by $f(x)=x^2$ for $x\le1$ and $f(x)=ax+b$ for $x>1$. (a) Find $a$ and $b$ so that $f$ is continuous and differentiable at $x=1$. [4] (b) The function $g(x)=|x^2-4|$ has a corner at $x=2$. Find the left and right gradients there and explain why $g$ is not differentiable at $x=2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) continuity: $a+b=1$ [M1][A1] differentiability: $2\times1=a$ [M1] $a=2$, $b=-1$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) left of $2$: $g=4-x^2$, gradient $-2x=-4$ [A1] right of $2$: $g=x^2-4$, gradient $2x=4$ [A1] the gradients differ, so no derivative exists [R1] [3 marks]
tips: For a smooth join, the two pieces must meet and have equal gradients at the joining point.

subtopic: Minimum average cost occurs where marginal cost equals average cost
statement: The total cost of producing $x$ items is $C(x)=x^3-6x^2+20x+32$ dollars, for $x>0$. The average cost is $A(x)=\dfrac{C(x)}x$ and the marginal cost is $C'(x)$. (a) Show that $A'(x)=\dfrac{C'(x)-A(x)}x$. [2] (b) Hence explain why, at the minimum of the average cost, the marginal cost equals the average cost. [1] (c) Show that the average cost is minimized at $x=4$, and find the minimum average cost. [4]
tips: Use the quotient rule on $C(x)/x$. Setting the derivative to zero links the three quantities.

subtopic: Using a derivative to prove an inequality
statement: Let $f(x)=e^x-1-x$ for all real $x$. (a) Show that $f$ has a single stationary point, and that it is a minimum. [3] (b) Hence show that $e^x\ge1+x$ for all real $x$, with equality only when $x=0$. [2] (c) By substituting $x=\dfrac1n$, show that $\left(1+\dfrac1n\right)^n<e$ for every positive integer $n$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=e^x-1=0$ at $x=0$ only [M1][A1] $f''(x)=e^x>0$ so a minimum [R1] [3 marks] (b) the minimum value is $f(0)=0$ [A1] so $f(x)\ge0$, with equality only at $x=0$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $1+\dfrac1n<e^{1/n}$ [M1] raise both sides to the power $n$ (positive) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A global minimum value of zero shows the function is never negative.

subtopic: Point where the gradient of a cubic is least
statement: The curve $C$ has equation $y=x^3-6x^2+9x$. (a) Find the gradient function $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and its minimum value. [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the point on $C$ where the gradient is least, and show that it is a point of inflection. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3x^2-12x+9$ [A1] minimum at $x=2$ [M1] $12-24+9=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $y=8-24+18=2$, so the point is $(2,2)$ [A1] $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-12$ [M1] it changes sign at $x=2$, so inflection [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The gradient is least where its own derivative, the second derivative of $y$, is zero.

subtopic: Greatest and least values of a cubic on a closed interval
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+5$ for $-2\le x\le4$. (a) Find the values of $x$ at which $f'(x)=0$. [2] (b) Find the greatest value and the least value of $f$ on the interval, and state the range of $f$. [4]
tips: On a closed interval, compare the values at the stationary points with the values at both end points.

subtopic: Linear approximation using the tangent line
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt x$. (a) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at $x=25$. [3] (b) Use the tangent to estimate $\sqrt{26}$. [1] (c) Using the sign of $f''(x)$, state whether $5.1$ is an overestimate or an underestimate, and give a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $f'(x)=\dfrac1{2\sqrt x}$ [A1] $f'(25)=\dfrac1{10}$ [A1] $y=5+\dfrac{x-25}{10}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $5+\dfrac1{10}=5.1$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $f''(x)=-\dfrac14x^{-3/2}<0$, so the graph is concave down [A1] the tangent lies above the curve, so $5.1$ is an overestimate [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Near $x=a$, $f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$. A concave-down curve lies below its tangent lines.

subtopic: The function ln x over x and the number of solutions of ln x = kx
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln x}x$ for $x>0$. You may use that $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ and $f(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$. (a) Show that $f'(x)=\dfrac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$, and hence find the coordinates and nature of the stationary point of $f$. [4] (b) Hence find, in terms of $k$, the number of solutions of $\ln x=kx$. [4] (c) Show that $e^\pi>\pi^e$. [3] (d) Verify that $f(2)=f(4)$. Explain why, if $a<b$ are positive integers with $a^b=b^a$, then $f(a)=f(b)$ and $a<e<b$, and deduce that $a=2$. [3]
markscheme: (a) quotient rule: $\dfrac{\frac1x\times x-\ln x}{x^2}$ [M1][A1] $=0$ at $\ln x=1$, so $x=e$ [A1] $f'$ is positive then negative, so a maximum at $\left(e,\dfrac1e\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\ln x=kx$ is the same as $f(x)=k$ [M1] $k>\dfrac1e$: none [A1] $k=\dfrac1e$: one [A1] $0<k<\dfrac1e$: two, and $k\le0$: one [A1] [4 marks] (c) $\pi>e$ and $f$ is decreasing for $x>e$, so $f(\pi)<f(e)$ [M1] $\dfrac{\ln\pi}\pi<\dfrac1e$, so $e\ln\pi<\pi$ [A1] $\pi^e<e^\pi$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\dfrac{\ln2}2=\dfrac{\ln4}4$ [A1] $b\ln a=a\ln b$ gives $f(a)=f(b)$, and $f$ is increasing for $x<e$ and decreasing for $x>e$, so $a<e<b$ [R1] $a$ is $1$ or $2$; $a=1$ would give $1=b$, impossible, so $a=2$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite the equation $\ln x=kx$ as $f(x)=k$ and count intersections with the horizontal line $y=k$. Decreasing functions preserve the order of their inputs.

subtopic: Longest pipe that can turn a corner
statement: A straight pipe is carried around a right-angled corner from a corridor of width $1$ m into a corridor of width $8$ m. A pipe that touches the inner corner and both outer walls at angle $\theta$ to the wider corridor's wall has length $L(\theta)=\dfrac1{\sin\theta}+\dfrac8{\cos\theta}$ for $0<\theta<\dfrac\pi2$. The longest pipe that can be turned around the corner has length equal to the minimum value of $L$. (a) Show that $L'(\theta)=0$ when $\tan^3\theta=\dfrac18$. [4] (b) Hence find the exact minimum value of $L$. [3] (c) Justify that this stationary value is a minimum. [2] (d) State the length of the longest pipe that can be carried around the corner, to three significant figures. [1] (e) For corridors of widths $a$ and $b$, so that $L=\dfrac a{\sin\theta}+\dfrac b{\cos\theta}$, show that the minimum value of $L$ is $\left(a^{2/3}+b^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $L'(\theta)=-\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{8\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta}$ [M1][A1] set to zero: $8\sin^3\theta=\cos^3\theta$ [M1] $\tan^3\theta=\dfrac18$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\tan\theta=\dfrac12$ so $\sin\theta=\dfrac1{\sqrt5}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac2{\sqrt5}$ [M1][A1] $L=\sqrt5+4\sqrt5=5\sqrt5$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $L\to\infty$ as $\theta\to0^+$ and as $\theta\to\dfrac\pi2^-$ [R1] there is only one stationary point, so it is the minimum [R1] [2 marks] (d) $5\sqrt5=11.2$ m [A1] [1 mark] (e) $\tan^3\theta=\dfrac ab$ so $\tan\theta=\dfrac{a^{1/3}}{b^{1/3}}$ [M1] $\sin\theta=\dfrac{a^{1/3}}{\sqrt S}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{b^{1/3}}{\sqrt S}$ with $S=a^{2/3}+b^{2/3}$ [A1] $L=a^{2/3}\sqrt S+b^{2/3}\sqrt S$ [M1] $=S^{3/2}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The longest pipe that fits is the smallest of the possible lengths $L(\theta)$, since it must fit at every angle.

subtopic: Separable equation whose solution has a restricted domain
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{x+y}$, with $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $-e^{-y}=e^x+C$ for a constant $C$, and find $C$. [3] (b) Find $y$ in terms of $x$, and state the largest set of values of $x$ for which the solution is defined. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^xe^y$ so $\int e^{-y}\,dy=\int e^x\,dx$ [M1] $-e^{-y}=e^x+C$ [AG] [A1] $-1=1+C$ so $C=-2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $e^{-y}=2-e^x$ [A1] $y=-\ln\left(2-e^x\right)$ [A1] $2-e^x>0$ so $x<\ln2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$ and separate the variables. The logarithm in the final answer needs a positive argument.

subtopic: Separable equation with inverse tangent solutions
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+y^2}{1+x^2}$, with $y=1$ when $x=0$. (a) Show that $\arctan y=\arctan x+C$ for some constant $C$, and find $C$. [4] (b) Show that $y=\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$, for $-1<x<1$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int\dfrac{dy}{1+y^2}=\int\dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$ [M1][A1] $\arctan y=\arctan x+C$ [AG] $\arctan1=\arctan0+C$ [M1] $C=\dfrac\pi4$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=\tan\left(\arctan x+\dfrac\pi4\right)$ [M1] $=\dfrac{x+1}{1-x\times1}$ using the compound angle formula for tangent [M1][A1] [3 marks]
tips: Both sides integrate to inverse tangents. Take the tangent of both sides and apply the compound angle formula.

subtopic: Loan balance with continuous interest and repayments
statement: The balance $A$ dollars of a loan at time $t$ years satisfies $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=0.05A-2000$, with $A=30\,000$ when $t=0$. (a) Explain the meaning of each of the two terms on the right-hand side. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $A=40\,000-10\,000e^{0.05t}$. [4] (c) Find, in years to three significant figures, when the loan is fully repaid. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.05A$: interest is added continuously at $5\%$ of the balance [A1] $-2000$: repayments at a constant rate of $\$2000$ per year [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dA}{0.05A-2000}=\int dt$ [M1] $20\ln|0.05A-2000|=t+c$ [A1] $0.05A-2000=-500e^{0.05t}$ using $t=0$ [M1] $A=40\,000-10\,000e^{0.05t}$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (c) $40\,000=10\,000e^{0.05t}$ [M1] $t=20\ln4=27.7$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The equation separates after factoring out $0.05$. The loan is repaid when the balance reaches zero.

subtopic: Orthogonal trajectories of a family of parabolas
statement: A family of curves is given by $y=cx^2$, where $c$ is a constant. (a) Show that every curve in the family satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}x$. [2] (b) Write down the differential equation satisfied by the curves that cross every member of the family at right angles, and solve it. [5] (c) Find the member of the perpendicular family that passes through $(2,1)$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2cx$ [M1] and $c=\dfrac y{x^2}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}x$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) perpendicular gradient $-\dfrac x{2y}$ so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac x{2y}$ [M1][A1] $\int2y\,dy=-\int x\,dx$ [M1] $y^2=-\dfrac{x^2}2+k$ [A1] $x^2+2y^2=K$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $4+2=6$, so $x^2+2y^2=6$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Two curves are perpendicular where their gradients multiply to $-1$. The perpendicular family satisfies the negative reciprocal gradient equation.

subtopic: Falling body with a resistance proportional to speed
statement: A body falls from rest, and its speed $v$ m/s after $t$ seconds satisfies $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=9.8-0.4v$. (a) Find the terminal speed. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $v=24.5\left(1-e^{-0.4t}\right)$. [4] (c) Find the time taken to reach $90\%$ of the terminal speed. [2]
tips: The equation is separable. Factor the right-hand side as a multiple of $24.5-v$ to integrate easily.

subtopic: A dissolving sugar cube with a surface-area rate law
statement: A sugar cube dissolves so that its volume $V$ cm$^3$ at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-0.5V^{2/3}$. Initially $V=27$. (a) Show that $V^{1/3}=3-\dfrac t6$. [4] (b) Find the time at which the volume has reduced to one eighth of its initial value. [2] (c) Find the time at which the cube has completely dissolved. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\int V^{-2/3}\,dV=-\int0.5\,dt$ [M1] $3V^{1/3}=-0.5t+c$ [A1] $c=3\times3=9$ [M1] $V^{1/3}=3-\dfrac t6$ [AG] [A1] [4 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac{27}8$ so $V^{1/3}=\dfrac32$ [M1] $t=6\left(3-\dfrac32\right)=9$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) $V=0$ when $t=18$ minutes [A1] [1 mark]
tips: The right-hand side is a power of $V$, so separate and integrate with a power rule. Note that the cube dissolves in a finite time.

subtopic: First-order linear equation with a repeated exponential
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=e^{-2x}$, with $y=3$ when $x=0$. (a) Find the integrating factor and use it to show that $\dfrac d{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right)=1$. [3] (b) Hence solve the differential equation. [3]
markscheme: (a) integrating factor $e^{\int2\,dx}=e^{2x}$ [A1] multiply the equation by $e^{2x}$ [M1] $\dfrac d{dx}\left(ye^{2x}\right)=e^{2x}e^{-2x}=1$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $ye^{2x}=x+C$ [M1] $C=3$ [A1] $y=(x+3)e^{-2x}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: After multiplying by the integrating factor, the left side is a product derivative and the right side simplifies.

subtopic: Separable equation with a quotient involving x squared plus one
statement: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{xy}{x^2+1}$ given that $y=3$ when $x=0$. Find $y$ in terms of $x$. [5]
markscheme: $\int\dfrac{dy}y=\int\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx$ [M1] $\ln|y|=\dfrac12\ln(x^2+1)+c$ [A1] $y=A\sqrt{x^2+1}$ [A1] $A=3$ [M1] $y=3\sqrt{x^2+1}$, valid for all real $x$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The $x$ integral is of the form $f'(x)/f(x)$. Take exponentials and combine the constant into one multiplier.

subtopic: A curve whose normal always passes through the origin
statement: A curve passes through the point $(3,4)$. At every point $(x,y)$ on the curve, the normal to the curve passes through the origin. (a) Show that the curve satisfies $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac xy$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to find the equation of the curve, and describe the curve. [4]
markscheme: (a) the normal has the gradient of the line from the origin to $(x,y)$, which is $\dfrac yx$ [M1] the tangent gradient is the negative reciprocal, $-\dfrac xy$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int y\,dy=-\int x\,dx$ [M1] $y^2=-x^2+c$ [A1] $c=25$ so $x^2+y^2=25$ [A1] a circle with centre at the origin and radius $5$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The normal and tangent are perpendicular. Use the fact that the line from the origin to the point has gradient $y/x$.

subtopic: Substitution u = x + y in a differential equation
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=(x+y)^2$, with $y=0$ when $x=0$. (a) Let $u=x+y$. Show that $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1+u^2$. [2] (b) Hence find $y$ in terms of $x$, for $-\dfrac\pi2<x<\dfrac\pi2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1+\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ [M1] $=1+u^2$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{du}{1+u^2}=\int dx$ [M1] $\arctan u=x+c$ [A1] $u=0$ at $x=0$ so $c=0$ [M1] $u=\tan x$ so $y=\tan x-x$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The substitution turns the equation into a separable equation in $u$ and $x$.

subtopic: Heating towards a steady state
statement: The temperature $T$ $^\circ$C of a pan on a hot plate at time $t$ minutes satisfies $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.1(T-20)+2$, where $20^\circ$C is the room temperature. Initially $T=25$. (a) Show that the differential equation can be written $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-0.1(T-40)$, and state the steady-state temperature. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation to show that $T=40-15e^{-0.1t}$. [3] (c) Find the time taken for the pan to reach $35^\circ$C, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $-0.1T+2+2=-0.1T+4=-0.1(T-40)$ [M1] steady-state temperature $40^\circ$C [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\int\dfrac{dT}{T-40}=-0.1\int dt$ [M1] $T-40=Ae^{-0.1t}$ [A1] $A=-15$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $15e^{-0.1t}=5$ [M1] $t=10\ln3=11.0$ minutes [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Combine the constants so that the equation has the form $dT/dt=-k(T-T_s)$ with steady state $T_s$.

subtopic: Growth rate proportional to the square root of the population
statement: The size $N$ of a colony at time $t$ hours satisfies $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k\sqrt N$, where $k>0$. At $t=0$, $N=400$, and at $t=4$, $N=900$. (a) Show that $\sqrt N=20+\dfrac{kt}2$. [3] (b) Find $k$, and the time when the colony reaches $2500$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\int N^{-1/2}\,dN=\int k\,dt$ [M1] $2\sqrt N=kt+c$ [A1] $c=40$ so $\sqrt N=20+\dfrac{kt}2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $30=20+2k$ so $k=5$ [A1] $\sqrt N=20+2.5t$ [M1] $50=20+2.5t$ so $t=12$ hours [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the power rule to integrate $N^{-1/2}$. The two data points fix the two constants.

subtopic: Mixing in a tank whose volume increases
statement: A tank initially contains $100$ L of solution with $20$ g of dissolved salt. A solution containing $2$ g of salt per liter flows in at $3$ L/min, and the well-mixed solution flows out at $1$ L/min. Let $S$ grams be the amount of salt at time $t$ minutes. (a) Show that the volume of liquid in the tank is $V=100+2t$ liters, and that $\dfrac{dS}{dt}=6-\dfrac S{100+2t}$. [3] (b) Find the integrating factor, and show that $\dfrac d{dt}\left(S\sqrt{100+2t}\right)=6\sqrt{100+2t}$. [3] (c) Solve the differential equation to show that $S=2(100+2t)-\dfrac{1800}{\sqrt{100+2t}}$. [4] (d) Find the amount of salt and the concentration in g/L when $t=50$. [2] (e) Show that the concentration is $2-\dfrac{1800}{(100+2t)^{3/2}}$, and find when it first reaches $1.5$ g/L. [3]
markscheme: (a) volume increases at $3-1=2$ L/min [A1] salt in: $3\times2=6$ g/min [A1] salt out: $1\times\dfrac S{100+2t}$ g/min, giving the equation [A1] [3 marks] (b) integrating factor $e^{\int\frac{dt}{100+2t}}=e^{\frac12\ln(100+2t)}$ [M1][A1] $=\sqrt{100+2t}$ and multiply through [A1] [3 marks] (c) $S\sqrt{100+2t}=\int6\sqrt{100+2t}\,dt=2(100+2t)^{3/2}+C$ [M1][A1] $S=2(100+2t)+\dfrac C{\sqrt{100+2t}}$ [A1] $20=200+\dfrac C{10}$ so $C=-1800$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) $S=400-\dfrac{1800}{\sqrt{200}}=273$ g [A1] concentration $\dfrac{273}{200}=1.36$ g/L [A1] [2 marks] (e) divide $S$ by $V=100+2t$ [A1] $\dfrac{1800}{V^{3/2}}=0.5$ so $V=3600^{2/3}=235$ [M1] $t=\dfrac{235-100}2=67.4$ minutes [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The volume changes with time, so the outflow of salt depends on $t$ through $S/V$. Use an integrating factor for the resulting linear equation.

subtopic: Equation involving a logarithm and its reciprocal
statement: For $a,b>0$ with $a,b\ne1$, consider the logarithms $\log_ab$ and $\log_ba$. (a) Show that $\log_ab=\dfrac1{\log_ba}$. [2] (b) Hence solve $\log_x3+\log_3x=\dfrac52$. [4]
markscheme: (a) let $\log_ab=p$, so $a^p=b$ [M1] then $a=b^{1/p}$, so $\log_ba=\dfrac1p$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (b) let $u=\log_3x$: $u+\dfrac1u=\dfrac52$ [M1] $2u^2-5u+2=0$ [A1] $u=2$ or $u=\dfrac12$ [A1] $x=9$ or $x=\sqrt3$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Let $u=\log_3x$ and use $\log_x3=1/u$. This gives a quadratic in $u$.

subtopic: Doubling time and the rule of 70
statement: A quantity grows by $r\%$ each year, so that after $t$ years it is multiplied by $\left(1+\dfrac r{100}\right)^t$. (a) Show that the doubling time is $\dfrac{\ln2}{\ln\left(1+\frac r{100}\right)}$ years. [2] (b) Find the doubling time for $r=2$, $r=5$ and $r=25$, each to three significant figures, and compare with $\dfrac{70}r$. [4] (c) A population grows continuously according to $P=P_0e^{kt}$ with the same annual growth factor as $3\%$ per year. Find $k$ to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\left(1+\dfrac r{100}\right)^t=2$ [M1] take logarithms [A1] [2 marks] (b) $r=2$: $35.0$ years, compared with $35$ [A1] $r=5$: $14.2$ years, compared with $14$ [A1] $r=25$: $3.11$ years, compared with $2.8$ [A1] the rule is accurate for small $r$ and less accurate for large $r$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $e^k=1.03$ [M1] $k=\ln1.03=0.0296$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The doubling time depends only on the growth factor, not on the initial amount.

subtopic: The logistic function e^x/(1+e^x): range, symmetry and inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. (a) Show that $f(-x)=1-f(x)$, and state the geometric meaning of this property. [3] (b) Find the range of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and its domain. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(-x)=\dfrac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}=\dfrac1{e^x+1}$ [M1][A1] $1-f(x)=\dfrac1{1+e^x}$ and the geometric meaning: rotational symmetry (half-turn) about $\left(0,\tfrac12\right)$ [R1] [3 marks] (b) $0<\dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}=1-\dfrac1{1+e^x}<1$ [M1] range $(0,1)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y(1+e^x)=e^x$ so $e^x(1-y)=y$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=\ln\dfrac x{1-x}$ [A1] domain $0<x<1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite $f$ as $1-\dfrac1{1+e^x}$ to see the range. For the inverse, swap $x$ and $y$ and make the exponential the subject.

subtopic: The pH scale and logarithms
statement: The pH of a solution is defined by $\text{pH}=-\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$, where $[\text{H}^+]$ is the concentration of hydrogen ions in mol/L. (a) Find $[\text{H}^+]$ for a solution with pH $3.5$, in the form $a\times10^k$ with $1\le a<10$. [2] (b) Find the pH of a solution with $[\text{H}^+]=0.002$ mol/L. [2] (c) Solution $A$ has pH $3$ and solution $B$ has pH $5$. Find how many times greater $[\text{H}^+]$ is in $A$ than in $B$. [2] (d) Equal volumes of solutions with $[\text{H}^+]=0.01$ and $[\text{H}^+]=0.001$ are mixed. Find the pH of the mixture, and explain why it is not the mean of the two pH values. [3]
markscheme: (a) $[\text{H}^+]=10^{-3.5}$ [M1] $=3.16\times10^{-4}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $-\log_{10}0.002$ [M1] $=2.70$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-5}}$ [M1] $=100$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) mixture concentration $\dfrac{0.01+0.001}2=0.0055$ [A1] pH $=2.26$ [A1] the pH scale is logarithmic, so averaging concentrations is not the same as averaging pH values (mean of pH values would be $2.5$) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A change of one pH unit corresponds to a factor of ten in concentration.

subtopic: Proving two logarithm identities
statement: Let $a,b,c$ be positive real numbers with $a,b\ne1$. (a) Show that $a^{\log_bc}=c^{\log_ba}$. [3] (b) Hence show that $2^{\log_57}=7^{\log_52}$. [2] (c) Use the change of base formula to show that $\log_ab\times\log_bc\times\log_ca=1$. [2]
markscheme: (a) let $x=a^{\log_bc}$; then $\log_bx=\log_bc\times\log_ba$ [M1][A1] by symmetry $\log_b\left(c^{\log_ba}\right)=\log_ba\times\log_bc$, so the two quantities are equal [A1] [3 marks] (b) apply the result with $a=2$, $b=5$, $c=7$ [M1] $2^{\log_57}=7^{\log_52}$ [AG] [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}\times\dfrac{\ln c}{\ln b}\times\dfrac{\ln a}{\ln c}$ [M1] $=1$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Take $\log_b$ of both sides. Each side then becomes the product $\log_bc\times\log_ba$.

subtopic: Intersections of an exponential and a quadratic
statement: Consider the functions $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=x^2$. (a) Use your calculator to find all solutions of $2^x=x^2$, giving the solution that is not an integer to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the set of values of $x$ for which $2^x<x^2$. [2] (c) State, with a reason, which function is greater for very large $x$. [1]
markscheme: (a) integer solutions $x=2$ and $x=4$ [A1][A1] non-integer solution $x=-0.767$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $2^x<x^2$ for $x<-0.767$ and for $2<x<4$ [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c) $2^x$, because exponential growth eventually exceeds any polynomial growth [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Plot both graphs and find every intersection. Check the sign of the difference between consecutive intersections.

subtopic: Solving ln(x squared) and the lost negative solution
statement: Consider the equation $\ln\left(x^2\right)=4$. (a) Solve the equation, giving exact values. [3] (b) A student writes $\ln\left(x^2\right)=2\ln x$ and obtains only one solution. Explain the error. [1] (c) Solve $\ln(x^2-1)=\ln(3)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x^2=e^4$ [M1] $x=\pm e^2$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $\ln x$ requires $x>0$, so the step loses the negative solution; correctly $\ln\left(x^2\right)=2\ln|x|$ [R1] [1 mark] (c) $x^2-1=3$ [M1] $x=\pm2$ (both satisfy $x^2-1>0$) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The logarithm of a square is defined for negative $x$ as well, but $2\ln x$ is not.

subtopic: Number of digits and leading digit using logarithms
statement: A positive integer $N$ has $k$ digits if $10^{k-1}\le N<10^k$. (a) Show that the number of digits of $N$ is $\lfloor\log_{10}N\rfloor+1$. [2] (b) Find the number of digits of $2^{100}$. [2] (c) Find the number of digits and the leading digit of $3^{100}$. [3]
tips: Write $N=10^{\log_{10}N}$. The fractional part of the logarithm determines the leading digits.

subtopic: Solving equations with exponentials and logarithms graphically
statement: Use your calculator to solve each equation, giving answers to three significant figures. (a) $e^x=4-x$. [2] (b) $\ln x=2-x^2$. [2] (c) Explain why each equation has exactly one solution. [2]
markscheme: (a) graph $y=e^x$ and $y=4-x$ [M1] $x=1.07$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) intersection of $y=\ln x$ and $y=2-x^2$ [M1] $x=1.31$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $e^x$ is increasing and $4-x$ is decreasing, so they cross only once [R1] $\ln x$ is increasing and $2-x^2$ is decreasing for $x>0$, so they cross only once [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Sketch both sides of the equation as functions and use the intersection tool on your calculator.

subtopic: Two exponential decay terms and when they are equal
statement: Two radioactive samples have activities (in counts per second) $A(t)=800e^{-0.3t}$ and $B(t)=200e^{-0.1t}$, where $t$ is in hours. (a) Show that $A(t)=B(t)$ when $e^{0.2t}=4$, and hence find $t$. [3] (b) State which sample has the greater activity for $t>6.93$, with a reason. [1] (c) Find the time at which the combined activity $A+B$ equals $500$ counts per second, to three significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $800e^{-0.3t}=200e^{-0.1t}$ [M1] $e^{0.2t}=4$ [AG] [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln4}{0.2}=6.93$ hours [A1] [3 marks] (b) $B$, since $A$ decays faster (larger decay rate $0.3>0.1$) [R1] [1 mark] (c) solve $800e^{-0.3t}+200e^{-0.1t}=500$ on the calculator [M1] $t=2.77$ hours [A1] check at $t=0$: total $1000$, decreasing, so a unique solution [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide both sides of the equation by one exponential to combine them. For the sum, use the numerical solver.

subtopic: Finding the constants of y = a b^x from two points
statement: The graph of $y=ab^x$, where $a>0$ and $b>1$, passes through the points $(2,12)$ and $(5,96)$. (a) Find the values of $a$ and $b$. [4] (b) Find the value of $x$ for which $y=100$, to three significant figures. [2]
tips: Dividing the two equations eliminates $a$.

subtopic: Simultaneous exponential equations with a reciprocal power
statement: The curves $y=3^x$ and $y=2\times3^{-x}+1$ intersect at one point. (a) Show that at the intersection $\left(3^x\right)^2-3^x-2=0$. [2] (b) Hence find the exact coordinates of the point of intersection. [4]
tips: Let $u=3^x$ and note that $u>0$, which removes one root.

subtopic: Sum of a geometric series of exponentials
statement: Consider the series $S=e^{-1}+e^{-2}+e^{-3}+\cdots$ (a) Show that the series converges and that its sum to infinity is $\dfrac1{e-1}$. [3] (b) Find the smallest number of terms $N$ for which the sum of the first $N$ terms exceeds $0.58$. [3]
markscheme: (a) geometric with first term $e^{-1}$ and ratio $e^{-1}$, and $|e^{-1}|<1$ [A1] $S_\infty=\dfrac{e^{-1}}{1-e^{-1}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac1{e-1}$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $S_N=\dfrac{1-e^{-N}}{e-1}$ [A1] $0.5805>0.58>0.5781$ for $N=6$ and $N=5$ [M1] $N=6$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The ratio $e^{-1}\approx0.368$ has modulus less than 1, so the series converges.

subtopic: Logarithmic equation leading to a quadratic
statement: Solve $\log_2(x+3)=3-\log_2x$. Find the exact value of $x$. [5]
markscheme: $\log_2(x+3)+\log_2x=3$ [M1] $\log_2\left(x(x+3)\right)=3$ so $x^2+3x=8$ [M1][A1] $x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{41}}2$ [A1] reject the negative root since $x>0$: $x=\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{41}}2$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: Combine the logarithms using the product law, convert to exponential form, and check the domain $x>0$.

subtopic: Compound interest and the limit definition of e to the r
statement: An amount is invested for one year at an annual rate $r$ (as a decimal), compounded $n$ times per year, so the growth factor is $\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)^n$. (a) By writing $h=\dfrac1n$, show that $\ln\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)^n=\dfrac{\ln(1+rh)}h$. [1] (b) Use l'Hôpital's rule to find $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0^+}\dfrac{\ln(1+rh)}h$, and deduce that $\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)^n\to e^r$ as $n\to\infty$. [4] (c) For $r=0.06$, find the growth factor for monthly compounding ($n=12$) and for continuous compounding, each to six significant figures. [3] (d) Using $\ln(1+x)\le x$ for $x>-1$, show that $\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)^n\le e^r$ for every $n$ when $r>0$. [3] (e) Find the growth factor for daily compounding ($n=365$) with $r=0.06$ to six significant figures, and comment. [2]
markscheme: (a) $n\ln\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)=\dfrac{\ln(1+rh)}h$ [AG] [A1] [1 mark] (b) limit is of the form $\dfrac00$ [M1] differentiate numerator and denominator: $\dfrac{r/(1+rh)}1$ [A1] $\to r$ [A1] so the growth factor tends to $e^r$ by continuity of the exponential [A1] [4 marks] (c) $n=12$: $1.00500^{12}$ [M1] $1.06168$ [A1] continuous: $e^{0.06}=1.06184$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $n\ln\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)\le n\times\dfrac rn=r$ [M1][A1] exponentiate: $\left(1+\dfrac rn\right)^n\le e^r$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $1.06183$ [A1] this is very close to, and below, the continuous value $1.06184$, as shown in part (d) [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The logarithm turns the power into a product, and l'Hôpital's rule handles the resulting $0/0$ limit.

subtopic: Leading digits and the logarithmic distribution
statement: In many real data sets the leading digit $D\in\{1,2,\ldots,9\}$ of a number occurs with probability $P(D=d)=\log_{10}\left(1+\dfrac1d\right)$. (a) Show that these probabilities sum to $1$. [3] (b) Find $P(D=1)$ and $P(D=9)$, each to three significant figures. [2] (c) Find $P(D\le3)$ and $P(D\ge5)$, giving exact answers in terms of logarithms. [3] (d) Find $E(D)$ to three significant figures. [2] (e) Show that a number $N>0$ has leading digit $d$ if and only if the fractional part of $\log_{10}N$ lies in $[\log_{10}d,\ \log_{10}(d+1))$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\log_{10}\dfrac{d+1}d=\log_{10}(d+1)-\log_{10}d$ [M1] the sum telescopes: $\log_{10}10-\log_{10}1$ [A1] $=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $P(D=1)=\log_{10}2=0.301$ [A1] $P(D=9)=\log_{10}\dfrac{10}9=0.0458$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P(D\le3)=\log_{10}4$ (telescoping) [M1][A1] $P(D\ge5)=\log_{10}\dfrac{10}5=\log_{10}2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\sum d\log_{10}\left(1+\dfrac1d\right)$ [M1] $=3.44$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) write $N=m\times10^k$ with $1\le m<10$ and $k$ an integer [M1] the leading digit is $d$ iff $d\le m<d+1$ [A1] $\log_{10}N=k+\log_{10}m$, so the fractional part is $\log_{10}m$, giving the result [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The sum of logarithms of consecutive ratios telescopes into a single logarithm.

subtopic: Inverse of a transformed function
statement: The function $f$ is one-to-one, and $g(x)=f(2x+1)-3$. (a) Show that $g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{f^{-1}(x+3)-1}2$. [3] (b) Given that $f(x)=x^3$, find $g^{-1}(5)$, and verify your answer by calculating $g$ of it. [3]
tips: Undo the operations in the reverse order: add 3, apply $f^{-1}$, subtract 1, divide by 2.

subtopic: Centre of symmetry of a cubic found by translation
statement: Let $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x$. (a) Show that $f(2+t)=t^3-3t+2$. [3] (b) Hence show that the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry (a half-turn) about the point $(2,2)$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(2+t)^3-6(2+t)^2+9(2+t)$ [M1] $=8+12t+6t^2+t^3-24-24t-6t^2+18+9t$ [A1] $=t^3-3t+2$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) $h(t)=f(2+t)-2=t^3-3t$ is the translated graph [M1] $h(-t)=-h(t)$, so $h$ is odd [A1] an odd function has rotational symmetry about the origin, so $y=f(x)$ has it about $(2,2)$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Translate the graph so that the suspected centre of symmetry is at the origin, and test whether the new function is odd.

subtopic: The graph of sin squared x as a transformation of cos x
statement: Consider the graph of $y=\sin^2x$. (a) Show that $\sin^2x=\dfrac12-\dfrac12\cos2x$. [2] (b) Describe a sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=\cos x$ onto the graph of $y=\sin^2x$. [4] (c) Write down the period, the maximum value and the minimum value of $\sin^2x$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x$ [M1] rearrange [A1] [2 marks] (b) horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] reflection in the $x$-axis [A1] translation by $\dfrac12$ upward [A1] [4 marks] (c) period $\pi$ [A1] maximum $1$ and minimum $0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use a double angle identity to remove the square, then read off the stretches, reflection and translation from the form $a\cos(bx)+c$.

subtopic: Areas under transformed graphs
statement: For a continuous function $f$, $\displaystyle\int_1^4f(x)\,dx=6$. (a) Find $\displaystyle\int_3^63f(x-2)\,dx$. [2] (b) Find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4}\left(f(x)+2\right)dx$. [2] (c) Find $\displaystyle\int_{1/2}^{2}f(2x)\,dx$. [2]
markscheme: (a) the graph is shifted $2$ to the right, so the limits $3$ to $6$ correspond to $1$ to $4$ [M1] $3\times6=18$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $6+2\times3$ [M1] $=12$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) let $u=2x$: $\dfrac12\int_1^4f(u)\,du$ [M1] $=3$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch by factor $1/2$ halves the area, a vertical stretch by $3$ triples it, and translations leave it unchanged.

subtopic: The normal density as a transformation of the standard curve
statement: The standard normal density is $\phi(z)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}$. The density of $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is $f(x)=\dfrac1\sigma\phi\left(\dfrac{x-\mu}\sigma\right)$. (a) Describe the sequence of transformations that maps the graph of $y=\phi(x)$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [3] (b) Find the maximum value of $f$ when $\sigma=2$, correct to three significant figures. [2] (c) Explain why the total area under the graph of $f$ is $1$ for every $\mu$ and $\sigma$. [2]
markscheme: (a) horizontal stretch with scale factor $\sigma$ [A1] translation $\mu$ to the right [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $\dfrac1\sigma$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac1{2\sqrt{2\pi}}$ [M1] $=0.199$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the horizontal stretch by $\sigma$ multiplies the area by $\sigma$ [R1] the vertical stretch by $\dfrac1\sigma$ cancels this, and the translation leaves the area unchanged [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A horizontal stretch scales area by the same factor as a vertical stretch does, so a pair of reciprocal stretches leaves the area unchanged.

subtopic: Choosing a translation that makes a function even
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2+bx+c$. (a) Find the value of $b$ for which $g(x)=f(x+2)$ is an even function. [3] (b) State the equation of the axis of symmetry of the graph of $y=f(x)$ for this value of $b$, and explain your answer. [2]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=x^2+(4+b)x+4+2b+c$ [M1][A1] even requires $4+b=0$, so $b=-4$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $x=2$ [A1] $g$ is even, so its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis; $f$ is $g$ translated $2$ units to the right [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The graph of $y=f(x+2)$ is the graph of $y=f(x)$ moved 2 units to the left.

subtopic: A logistic curve as a transformed function
statement: A population is modeled by $P(t)=\dfrac{1000}{1+e^{-r(t-12)}}$, where $t$ is in months and $r>0$. The population at $t=0$ is $100$. (a) Find the exact value of $r$, and its value to three significant figures. [3] (b) Find the population when $t=20$. [2] (c) Find the value of $t$ at which the population reaches $900$, and explain why the population is $500$ at $t=12$. [3]
tips: The factor $(t-12)$ translates the standard logistic curve 12 units to the right, so the midpoint is at $t=12$.

subtopic: Splitting a polynomial into even and odd parts
statement: Any function $f$ can be written as $f=E+O$, where $E(x)=\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}2$ and $O(x)=\dfrac{f(x)-f(-x)}2$. (a) Show that $E$ is even and $O$ is odd. [2] (b) Find $E(x)$ and $O(x)$ for $f(x)=x^3+2x^2-5x+1$. [3] (c) Find $E(x)$ and $O(x)$ for $f(x)=e^x$. [2]
tips: For a polynomial, the even part contains the even powers of $x$ and the odd part contains the odd powers.

subtopic: Transformations that give the same graph
statement: For some functions, a vertical stretch produces the same graph as a horizontal stretch or a translation. (a) Show that a vertical stretch of the graph of $y=x^3$ with scale factor $8$ gives the same graph as a horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$. [2] (b) Find the horizontal stretch that gives the same graph as the vertical stretch of $y=\sqrt x$ with scale factor $3$. [2] (c) Find the horizontal translation that gives the same graph as the vertical stretch of $y=e^x$ with scale factor $5$. [2] (d) Explain why no horizontal translation of $y=x^2$ gives the same graph as a vertical stretch of $y=x^2$ with scale factor $4$. [1]
markscheme: (a) vertical stretch: $y=8x^3$ [A1] horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$: $y=(2x)^3=8x^3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=3\sqrt x=\sqrt{9x}$ [M1] horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac19$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $5e^x=e^{x+\ln5}$ [M1] translation by $\ln5$ to the left [A1] [2 marks] (d) a translation moves the vertex, but the vertex of the stretched graph stays at the origin [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Rewrite the stretched equation in a form that looks like a horizontal change. Powers, roots and exponentials each have an identity that allows this.

subtopic: Showing that a graph has a line of symmetry
statement: A graph is symmetric about the line $x=a$ if $f(a+t)=f(a-t)$ for all $t$. (a) Show that the graph of $f(x)=x^2-6x+11$ is symmetric about $x=3$. [2] (b) Show that the graph of $y=\cos x$ is symmetric about $x=\pi$. [2] (c) Show that $g(x)=(x-1)(x-5)(x^2-6x+10)$ is symmetric about $x=3$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(3+t)=(3+t)^2-6(3+t)+11=t^2+2$ [M1] this is even in $t$, so $f(3+t)=f(3-t)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos(\pi+t)=-\cos t$ [M1] $\cos(\pi-t)=-\cos t$, so the values are equal [A1] [2 marks] (c) let $t=x-3$: $(t+2)(t-2)\left(t^2+1\right)$ [M1][A1] $=(t^2-4)(t^2+1)$ is even in $t$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Substitute $x=a+t$ and simplify. If the result contains only even powers of $t$, the graph is symmetric about $x=a$.

subtopic: A time delay as a vertical stretch of an exponential graph
statement: The value of an investment is $A(x)=1000\times1.05^x$ dollars after $x$ years. A second investment, delayed by $3$ years, has value $B(x)=A(x-3)$. (a) Show that $B(x)=k\times1.05^x$, and find $k$ to four significant figures. [3] (b) Describe the translation of the graph of $A$ that gives $B$, and the vertical stretch that gives the same graph. [2] (c) Find the delay $d$ for which $A(x-d)$ is exactly half of $A(x)$, to three significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $B(x)=1000\times1.05^{x-3}$ [M1] $=1000\times1.05^{-3}\times1.05^x$ [A1] $k=863.8$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) translation by $3$ units to the right [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $1.05^{-3}=0.864$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.05^{-d}=\dfrac12$ [M1] $d=\dfrac{\ln2}{\ln1.05}=14.2$ years [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $a^{x-3}=a^{-3}a^x$ to turn a horizontal shift into a vertical stretch.

subtopic: Different transformations mapping sine onto cosine
statement: Consider the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$. (a) Show that $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi2\right)$, and describe the translation that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [2] (b) Describe a translation followed by a reflection that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [3] (c) Describe a reflection followed by a translation that maps $y=\sin x$ onto $y=\cos x$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sin\left(x+\dfrac\pi2\right)=\sin x\cos\dfrac\pi2+\cos x\sin\dfrac\pi2=\cos x$ [M1] translation by $\dfrac\pi2$ to the left [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\cos x=-\sin\left(x-\dfrac\pi2\right)$ [M1] translation $\dfrac\pi2$ to the right [A1] reflection in the $x$-axis [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos x=\sin\left(\dfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin\left(-\left(x-\dfrac\pi2\right)\right)$ [M1] reflection in the $y$-axis [A1] translation $\dfrac\pi2$ to the right [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use the identity $\sin(\pi/2-x)=\cos x$ and check the order of the two transformations carefully.

subtopic: Stationary points under transformations of a graph
statement: The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a local minimum at $(3,-2)$ and a local maximum at $(-1,5)$. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is the image of $y=f(x)$ after the transformation $g(x)=-2f(x-1)+3$. (a) Find the coordinates of the image of the local minimum, and state whether it is a local minimum or a local maximum of $g$. [3] (b) Find the coordinates and nature of the image of the local maximum of $f$. [3] (c) Write $g'(x)$ in terms of $f'$, and explain why the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points are as found. [2]
markscheme: (a) $x=3+1=4$ [A1] $y=-2\times(-2)+3=7$ [A1] the reflection in the $x$-axis turns the minimum into a maximum [R1] [3 marks] (b) $x=-1+1=0$ [A1] $y=-2\times5+3=-7$ [A1] a local minimum, by the same reflection [R1] [3 marks] (c) $g'(x)=-2f'(x-1)$ [A1] $g'(x)=0$ when $f'(x-1)=0$, that is when $x-1=3$ or $x-1=-1$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A vertical stretch by a negative factor reflects the graph, so maxima and minima swap roles.

subtopic: Transformations of the square root function
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{4-2x}+1$. (a) Describe a sequence of four transformations that maps the graph of $y=\sqrt x$ onto the graph of $y=f(x)$. [4] (b) Write down the domain and range of $f$. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain. [3]
markscheme: (a) horizontal stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$, giving $\sqrt{2x}$ [A1] reflection in the $y$-axis, giving $\sqrt{-2x}$ [A1] translation by $2$ to the right, giving $\sqrt{-2(x-2)}=\sqrt{4-2x}$ [A1] translation by $1$ upward [A1] [4 marks] (b) domain $x\le2$ [A1] range $f(x)\ge1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(y-1)^2=4-2x$ [M1] $f^{-1}(x)=2-\dfrac{(x-1)^2}2$ [A1] domain $x\ge1$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Factor the expression under the root as $-2(x-2)$ to read off the stretch, reflection and translation.

subtopic: A sum of a function and its translated copy
statement: Let $f(x)=x^2$ and $h(x)=f(x)+f(x-2)$. (a) Show that $h(x)=2(x-1)^2+2$. [2] (b) State the coordinates of the vertex of the graph of $h$, and describe the transformations that map $y=x^2$ onto $y=h(x)$. [3] (c) Explain, using symmetry, why the vertex of $h$ lies at $x=1$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $h(x)=x^2+(x-2)^2=2x^2-4x+4$ [M1] $=2(x-1)^2+2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) vertex $(1,2)$ [A1] vertical stretch with scale factor $2$ [A1] translation $1$ to the right and $2$ up [A1] [3 marks] (c) the two parabolas have vertices at $x=0$ and $x=2$, and $h$ is symmetric about the midpoint $x=1$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Expand both squares, collect like terms and complete the square.

subtopic: Composing horizontal stretches and translations
statement: A horizontal stretch from the $y$-axis with scale factor $k>0$ changes $y=f(x)$ into $y=f\left(\dfrac xk\right)$. A horizontal translation of $c$ units to the right changes $y=f(x)$ into $y=f(x-c)$. In each case the new equation is obtained from the current one. (a) The graph of $y=f(x)$ is translated $3$ units to the right and then stretched horizontally with scale factor $2$. Show that the resulting equation is $y=f\left(\dfrac{x-6}2\right)$. [3] (b) Show that stretching with scale factor $k$ and then translating $c$ units right gives $y=f\left(\dfrac{x-c}k\right)$, and deduce that translating $c$ right and then stretching with scale factor $k$ is equivalent to stretching first and then translating $kc$ right. [4] (c) Describe, as a stretch followed by a translation, the single sequence that maps the graph of $y=f(x)$ onto the graph of $y=f(2x+5)$. [3] (d) Describe the same transformation as a translation followed by a stretch. [2] (e) Explain why $y=f(x)$ translated $2$ to the right and then stretched with scale factor $3$ is not the same graph as stretched first and then translated $2$ to the right, unless $f$ is constant. [1]
markscheme: (a) after the translation: $y=f(x-3)$ [A1] the stretch replaces $x$ by $\dfrac x2$: $y=f\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)$ [M1] $=f\left(\dfrac{x-6}2\right)$ [AG] [A1] [3 marks] (b) stretch: $f\left(\dfrac xk\right)$ then translation: $f\left(\dfrac{x-c}k\right)$ [A1] translate then stretch: $f\left(\dfrac xk-c\right)$ [M1] $=f\left(\dfrac{x-kc}k\right)$ [A1] this is a stretch followed by a translation of $kc$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) $f(2x+5)=f\left(\dfrac{x+5/2}{1/2}\right)$ [M1] stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] followed by a translation $\dfrac52$ to the left [A1] [3 marks] (d) $f(2x+5)=f\left(\dfrac{x}{1/2}+5\right)$ so the translation comes first [M1] translation $5$ to the left, then a stretch with scale factor $\dfrac12$ [A1] [2 marks] (e) the first gives $f\left(\dfrac x3-2\right)$ and the second gives $f\left(\dfrac{x-2}3\right)=f\left(\dfrac x3-\dfrac23\right)$, which are different translations of the graph [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Always apply the transformations to the current equation. A horizontal stretch replaces every $x$ in the current equation, including the translation inside it.

subtopic: Relationships between families of exponential and logarithmic graphs
