[3] (c) Find the angle above the positive $x$-axis at which the interceptor should be launched, to the nearest tenth of a degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) distance from the origin to the drone is $\sqrt{(10-2t)^2+t^2}$ [A1] this equals $5t$ at the meeting time [M1] $100-40t+5t^2=25t^2$, so $20t^2+40t-100=0$, that is $t^2+2t-5=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $t=-1+\sqrt6=1.45$ hours [A1] position $(10-2t,\ t)$ [M1] $=(7.10,\ 1.45)$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\tan\theta=\dfrac{1.449}{7.101}$ [M1] $\theta=11.5^\circ$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: At the interception time, the distance travelled by the interceptor equals the distance from the origin to the drone's position.

subtopic: Magnitude of a cross product and the identity with the dot product
statement: Let $\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ and verify that it is perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [4] (b) Verify that $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|^2=|\mathbf a|^2|\mathbf b|^2-(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b)^2$, and deduce the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}5\\ 5\\ -5\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=5+10-15=0$ [A1] $\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b)=10-5-5=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) left side $=75$; $|\mathbf a|^2=14$, $|\mathbf b|^2=6$, $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=3$, right side $84-9=75$ [A1] $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta$ gives $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{75}}{\sqrt{84}}$ [M1] $\theta=70.9^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The identity follows from $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$ with the dot product and cross product formulas.

subtopic: Resolving a force into components along and perpendicular to a direction
statement: A force $\mathbf F=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ -3\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ N acts on a particle. The particle can move only in the direction $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the component of $\mathbf F$ parallel to $\mathbf d$, as a vector. [3] (b) Find the component of $\mathbf F$ perpendicular to $\mathbf d$, and verify that it is perpendicular. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|^2}\mathbf d$ [M1] $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=12-3+4=13$ and $|\mathbf d|^2=9$ [A1] $\dfrac{13}9\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf F-\dfrac{13}9\mathbf d=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}28\\ -40\\ -8\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] dot product with $\mathbf d$: $56-40-16=0$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The parallel component is the projection of the force onto the direction. The remainder is perpendicular to the direction.

subtopic: Ratios in which two cevians of a triangle divide each other
statement: In triangle $ABC$, let $\overrightarrow{AB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf c$. The point $D$ lies on $BC$ with $BD:DC=1:2$, and $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$. The lines $AD$ and $BE$ meet at $P$. (a) Show that $\overrightarrow{AD}=\dfrac13(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$, and write down $\overrightarrow{AE}$. [3] (b) Write $\overrightarrow{AP}$ in two ways, using $\overrightarrow{AP}=\lambda\overrightarrow{AD}$ and $\overrightarrow{AP}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\mu\overrightarrow{BE}$, and find $\lambda$ and $\mu$. [5] (c) State the ratios $AP:PD$ and $BP:PE$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AD}=\mathbf b+\dfrac13(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)$ [M1] $=\dfrac13(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [AG] [A1] $\overrightarrow{AE}=\dfrac12\mathbf c$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AP}=\dfrac\lambda3(2\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{AP}=\mathbf b+\mu\left(\dfrac12\mathbf c-\mathbf b\right)=(1-\mu)\mathbf b+\dfrac\mu2\mathbf c$ [A1] $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ are not parallel, so compare coefficients: $\dfrac{2\lambda}3=1-\mu$ and $\dfrac\lambda3=\dfrac\mu2$ [M1] solve: $\lambda=\dfrac34$ [A1] $\mu=\dfrac12$ [A1] [5 marks] (c) $AP:PD=3:1$ and $BP:PE=1:1$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Take $A$ as the origin so that the two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ serve as a basis. Equate coefficients.

subtopic: Dividing a line segment externally
statement: The points $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(2,0,5)$ are given. The point $C$ lies on the line $AB$ beyond $B$, with $AC=3AB$. (a) Find the position vector of $C$. [3] (b) Find the ratio $AB:BC$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AC}=3\overrightarrow{AB}=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC}$, so $C=(4,-4,9)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $BC=2AB$, so $AB:BC=1:2$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Because $C$ is beyond $B$, the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ point in the same direction.

subtopic: Testing whether four points are coplanar
statement: The points are $A(1,0,0)$, $B(0,2,0)$ and $C(0,0,3)$. (a) Find the equation of the plane through $A$, $B$ and $C$ in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [4] (b) Determine whether each of $D(2,2,-6)$ and $E(1,1,1)$ lies in the plane $ABC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 0\\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] normal $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\ 3\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $6x+3y+2z=6$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $D$: $12+6-12=6$, so $D$ is in the plane [A1] $E$: $6+3+2=11\ne6$, so $E$ is not [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Four points are coplanar when the fourth lies on the plane through the other three.

subtopic: Reflection of a ray in a plane
statement: A light ray leaves the origin in the direction $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and hits the plane $\Pi$ with equation $x+2y+2z=9$. A ray with direction $\mathbf d$ reflects from a plane with normal $\mathbf n$ with new direction $\mathbf d'=\mathbf d-\dfrac{2(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n)}{|\mathbf n|^2}\mathbf n$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point $P$ where the ray meets $\Pi$. [3] (b) Find the direction of the reflected ray. [3] (c) Find the angle between the incoming ray and the normal to the plane, and show that $\mathbf d'$ has the same length as $\mathbf d$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(2t,2t,t)$ in the plane: $2t+4t+2t=9$ [M1] $t=\dfrac98$ [A1] $P=\left(\dfrac94,\dfrac94,\dfrac98\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=8$ and $|\mathbf n|^2=9$ [A1] $\mathbf d'=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 2\\ 1\end{pmatrix}-\dfrac{16}9\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\dfrac19\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -14\\ -23\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\cos\phi=\dfrac{8}{3\times3}$ [M1] $\phi=27.3^\circ$ [A1] $|\mathbf d'|^2=\dfrac{4+196+529}{81}=9=|\mathbf d|^2$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A reflection reverses the component of the direction along the normal and keeps the component in the plane.

subtopic: Plane containing a line and a point
statement: The line $L$ has equation $\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, and $Q$ is the point $(0,1,1)$. Find the equation of the plane that contains $L$ and $Q$, in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. [5]
markscheme: $A(1,0,2)$ is on $L$, $\overrightarrow{AQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] normal $=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $-x+y+2z=3$ using $A$ [M1] check with $Q$: $0+1+2=3$ [A1] [5 marks]
tips: The plane contains the direction of the line and the vector from a point on the line to $Q$, so the cross product of these gives its normal.

subtopic: Cartesian form of a line in three dimensions
statement: A line has equation $\dfrac{x-1}2=\dfrac{y+2}3=\dfrac{z-4}{-1}$. (a) Write down a point on the line and a direction vector. [2] (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the line meets the plane $z=0$. [3] (c) Show that the point $(3,1,3)$ lies on the line. [2]
markscheme: (a) $(1,-2,4)$ [A1] $\begin{pmatrix}2\\ 3\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) let the common value be $\lambda$, so $x=1+2\lambda$, $y=-2+3\lambda$, $z=4-\lambda$ [M1] $z=0$ gives $\lambda=4$ [A1] $(9,10,0)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac{3-1}2=1$, $\dfrac{1+2}3=1$ [M1] $\dfrac{3-4}{-1}=1$, all equal [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Set each ratio equal to a parameter to turn the Cartesian form into a vector equation.

subtopic: The orthocentre and the Euler line using position vectors
statement: Triangle $ABC$ has circumcentre at the origin $O$, so $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=|\mathbf c|=R$. The point $H$ has position vector $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$. (a) Show that $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$. [3] (b) Explain, by the same argument, why $H$ is the orthocentre of the triangle. [2] (c) The centroid $G$ has position vector $\dfrac13(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)$. Show that $O$, $G$, $H$ are collinear and find the ratio $OG:GH$. [3] (d) A triangle has vertices $A(5,0)$, $B(-3,4)$, $C(-3,-4)$, all on a circle of radius $5$ centered at the origin. Find $H$, and verify that $BH$ is perpendicular to $CA$. [4] (e) Find the position of $H$ for an equilateral triangle with circumcentre at $O$, and explain. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AH}=\mathbf b+\mathbf c$ [A1] $(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf b)=|\mathbf c|^2-|\mathbf b|^2$ [M1] $=0$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) similarly $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=0$ and $\overrightarrow{CH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=0$ [R1] $H$ lies on all three altitudes [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf h=3\mathbf g$ [A1] so $H$ lies on the line $OG$ [R1] $OG:GH=1:2$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\mathbf h=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{BH}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\overrightarrow{CA}=\begin{pmatrix}8\\ 4\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] dot product $16-16=0$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ by symmetry, so $H=O$, the centroid, circumcentre and orthocentre coincide [R1] [1 mark]
tips: With the circumcentre at the origin, the equal lengths of the position vectors make the dot products in the altitude condition cancel.

subtopic: A regular tetrahedron inscribed in a cube
statement: The points $A(1,1,1)$, $B(1,-1,-1)$, $C(-1,1,-1)$ and $D(-1,-1,1)$ are four vertices of a cube with vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, and $O$ is the origin. (a) Show that all six edges of $ABCD$ have length $2\sqrt2$. [2] (b) Find the angle $AOB$ between two vertices seen from the centre. [3] (c) Show that the plane through $A$, $B$, $C$ has equation $x+y-z=1$, and find the equation of the plane through $A$, $B$, $D$. [4] (d) The outward normals to the faces $ABC$ and $ABD$ are $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\\ -1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between these faces, explaining how it relates to the angle between the normals. [3] (e) The tetrahedron is obtained from the cube by removing four corner tetrahedra. Find its volume, and check it against the formula $V=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}s^3$ for a regular tetrahedron with edge $s$. [3]
markscheme: (a) e.g. $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}$ has length $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$ [A1] the other five edge vectors are $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ -2\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ -2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 2\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ 2\end{pmatrix}$, each with length $2\sqrt2$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}=1-1-1=-1$ [A1] $|\overrightarrow{OA}|^2=3$ [A1] $\cos AOB=-\dfrac13$, so $AOB=109.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -2\\ -2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}-2\\ 0\\ -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\ 4\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $x+y-z=1$ using $A$ [AG] plane $ABD$: $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AD}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ 4\\ -4\end{pmatrix}$, giving $-x+y-z=-1$ [A1][A1] [4 marks] (d) $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{1-1-1}{3}=-\dfrac13$ for the outward normals [A1] the angle between the faces is $180^\circ-\alpha$ [R1] $=\arccos\dfrac13=70.5^\circ$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) cube volume $2^3=8$ [A1] each corner tetrahedron has volume $\dfrac13\times\dfrac12\times2\times2\times2=\dfrac43$, so $V=8-4\times\dfrac43=\dfrac83$ [A1] $\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}\left(2\sqrt2\right)^3=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{12}\times16\sqrt2=\dfrac83$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Alternating vertices of a cube form a regular tetrahedron. The angle between faces is the angle between the normals when the normals point outward, subtracted from $180^\circ$.
